articles.title: The best way to cook bacon, according to chefs
articles.summary: Are those crispy strips best prepared on the stovetop or in the oven? Experts weigh in.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

I try to eat a healthy, well-balanced diet; I really do. But when it comes to bacon, I'm weak. Just the smell of it cooking is enough to get my salivary glands working overtime. I eat it for breakfast with toast and home fries; I eat it for lunch on a BLT; I eat it for dinner with a baked potato. I just love it so much.

Over the years, I've cooked my bacon any numbers of ways. These days, however, I have two go-to methods. I cook my strips on a sheet tray in the oven if I'm not in a rush. When time is of the essence, however, I plop it on a plate with some paper towels, toss it in the microwave, and it's ready in less than five minutes. I like it both ways, but there's no denying different cooking methods deliver different tastes and textures. Culinary experts agree, and it turns out they've got some strong opinions on the best and worst ways to cook bacon.

The consensus among all the chefs I spoke to? Baking bacon on sheet pan in the oven is your best bet.

"The oven is a great option because the bacon cooks gradually, so you still have a lot of fat in it, but it's crisp around the edges," explains Casey Bumpsteed , a chef and food stylist who qualified as a Cordon Bleu Chef at Silwood Kitchens in Cape Town, South Africa.

David McIntyre, the executive chef of Lana Restaurant in San Diego, Calif., is also a fan of this method because the bacon cooks evenly without you having to do much work. "You get a nice consistent result," he says.

Letting your strips sizzle away in the oven is also a great idea if you're cooking a big batch. But according to Nelson Castillo Quinones, the head of the kitchen at AmishView Inn & Suites in Lancaster County, Pa., there are some drawbacks. "For larger quantities, I prefer the oven. The downside is that it takes a little longer and doesn't give you quite the same immediate control as the stovetop," he says.

If you don't want your bacon to braise in its own fat while it cooks, place a cooling rack on top of your baking sheet before adding the bacon. When your bacon cooks on the cooling rack, the grease collects on the sheet pan below. Genius, right?

More than 1,000 shoppers have given these nonstick sheet pans a perfect five-star rating. Fans attest that food slides right off and that they're super easy to clean. "Excellent quality and perfect size variety," one customer shared . "Even heating and easy cleanup. Ideal for everyday baking."

If you only need a few pieces of bacon, frying it on the stovetop isn't a bad idea. The pros say cooking your bacon in a skillet allows you control the crispness and develop the flavor for seriously yummy results.

"When you cook bacon in a frying pan, do it on low heat so that the fat renders slowly, giving it a nice taste that's very savory," Bumpsteed recommends.

Michelle Doll Olsen, the head chef at HelloFresh and graduate of the French Culinary Institute, suggests using a cast iron skillet to up the deliciousness factor. "Start with cold strips in a cold pan and cook it low and slow over medium heat, flipping now and then until it hits the crispiness you like," she says. McIntyre is also a fan of this method, noting, " Cast iron is great if you want a little more caramelization."

Before you crank up your burners, one important note: The grease factor. Bumpsteed says cooking bacon this way will make it more greasy compared to the other methods. And let's not forget about all the splatter you'll need to clean off your stove.

Want to save yourself a big cleanup job? Invest in these simple yet handy mesh covers to place over your skillet to minimize the mess.

"Great for covering a pan when you are frying something. It definitely keeps the splatters from going all over your stove," one shopper shared .

If you're going to cook bacon low and slow like our experts recommend, you'll want a skillet that gives you plenty of control. This pre-seasoned cast-iron skillet is an affordable option that holds heat well and helps develop that flavorful browning the chefs love.

And it's got plenty of fans beyond the chefs we spoke with. Our resident cooking expert uses this skillet at home and praises its durability and versatility, while our expert testers named Lodge the best cast-iron skillet they tried. Even Ina Garten counts this pan among her kitchen must-haves.

Not sure you're ready to invest in a top-of-the-line stainless steel skillet just yet? Start with this fan favorite that's currently on sale for under $40. It has an ergonomic design and can be used on all cooktops.

"I’ve been using this pan for a while now, and I’m very impressed. It heats up evenly, cooks food beautifully, and nothing burns when used properly. The stainless steel feels sturdy and high quality, and the lid fits perfectly," one reviewer wrote .

Okay, now, the least favorite cooking method: The microwave. The experts agree on two things here. First, nuking your bacon is quick and relatively simple. Second, it does nothing to enhance the flavor.

Bumpsteed doesn't like microwaved bacon, and isn't afraid to say so. "Cooked this way, you are left with a dry piece of bacon that is not that tasty. The fat just renders quickly, and you absolutely must have fat in it to make it really good," she says.

Another reason to think twice about this cooking method? Not all bacon is designed to perform well in the microwave, cautions chef Barry Greenberg, the executive chef for Hormel Foodservice division. "Unless you're using pre-cooked or microwave-optimized bacon, results can be inconsistent," he says.

This contraption may look complicated, but it's actually quite simple to use. Just drape your bacon slices over the racks, place a paper towel on top, then pop the whole thing in the microwave. In just a few minutes, you'll have perfectly cooked (not greasy!) strips.

"This product makes cooking bacon in the microwave easy without a mess," one fan raved . "The bacon turns out great, the spout makes it easy to pour off the grease, and it's easy to clean with just some dish soap and water."

Worried about grease splatters? There's an option that comes with a lid .

articles.title: A woman boarded a United flight and realized she was the only passenger. Then the pilot made it unforgettable.
articles.summary: A Reddit user boarded a United Airlines flight, only to discover she was the sole passenger on board, prompting a private safety demonstration, the use of we...
articles.body:
A woman flying United from Huntsville to Houston on a Wednesday evening in June boarded the regional jet and found she had it to herself .

Under the username u/Sufficient_Fudge_280 , she later posted a photo of the empty plane on Reddit captioned, "Somehow the only person on my flight and the pilot was such a goofy goober."

She got her own personalized preflight announcements . The flight attendant also ran the full safety demonstration for an audience of one, laughing the whole way through it.

Before takeoff, the crew brought sandbags into the cabin. She wrote that it was "bc the plane was too light with only one passenger," though that isn't quite the reason. It's not that planes are too light to fly, but with an empty cabin, the center of gravity can shift, and that extra weight pulls it back in. On a small regional jet with one person aboard, sandbags are a normal way to solve that problem.

After landing and taxiing in, the captain invited her up to the flight deck to sit in the seat and look around.

"The crew was so cool," she wrote, adding that the whole thing was funny and joyful.

Reddit mostly enjoyed it, with one commenter calling it a "poor man's private jet." Another said, "I would have been freaking out at the gate, thinking I was in the wrong place because nobody else was there." A third quipped, "Still made her gate check her bag for lack of bin space."

articles.title: Toddler found dead inside temple with deep neck cut; elder brother arrested
articles.summary: Patna: 1.5-year-old boy found dead in Durga temple with deep neck cut; police arrest 24-year-old brother Ajit Kumar, probe motive and circumstances.
articles.body: PATNA: A one-and-a-half-year-old boy was allegedly murdered inside a Durga temple in Jeetan Chhapra village under Ranitalab police station area in Patna district on Saturday. A deep cut was found on his neck.Police arrested the child’s elder brother, 24-year-old Ajit Kumar, in connection with the murder.Paliganj sub-divisional police officer (SDPO-II) Pankaj Kumar Sharma said police received information about the murder at around 11.50am. After verifying the information, a police team reached the spot and, with the help of villagers, took Ajit into custody.The SDPO said Ajit, son of tractor driver Ranju Yadav, allegedly killed his younger brother Manish Kumar alias Hanuman with a ‘dabia’ (a sharp agricultural cutting weapon) inside the temple premises. Police are investigating the circumstances leading to the killing.Ranitalab SHO Navneet Anand told TOI the police had recovered the child’s body and were probing the circumstances surrounding the murder. “The accused is being questioned to establish the sequence of events and the motive behind the killing,” he said.Locals had earlier raised suspicion of a possible connection with witchcraft or a ritual, but police have not confirmed the motive. Investigators are examining all aspects of the case.An FSL team was called to the crime scene to collect evidence. Police said further details would emerge as the investigation progresses. articles.title: FIR filed after students allege ‘inappropriate touch’ by teacher in Rajasthan
articles.summary: FIR filed in Jaipur after Class 5-6 girls allege inappropriate touch by govt school teacher and acting principal; teacher placed under APO, inquiry ordered.

articles.title: ‘No line he will not cross’: Obama slams Ramaswamy’s ‘cruel’ ad, hits out at Trump
articles.summary: Former US President Barack Obama has criticised President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, accusing them of abandoning basic standards of decency
articles.body: Former US President Barack Obama has criticised President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, accusing them of abandoning basic standards of decency as he campaigned for Democratic candidates in Ohio ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.Obama focused much of his criticism on Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has continued to defend an advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Dr Amy Acton. Trump and vice president JD Vance have also defended the campaign, despite calls from prominent Ohio Republicans, including governor Mike DeWine, to withdraw it."In recent days, we have seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy. He noted that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she has experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness"."There is a decency we should expect out of our public officials," Obama continued. "And I do not know what has happened where the standards of behaviour are so low that somebody could run an ad like that."Acton accuses Ramaswamy of exploiting her childhoodActon, who appeared alongside Obama, directly challenged Ramaswamy over the advertisement, accusing him of using her personal history to rescue his campaign."My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it is not going to work," she said. "Decency still matters."She added: "Mr Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you will not stoop."Ramaswamy has defended the advertisement as legitimate campaign material, while the controversy has intensified an already closely fought election in Ohio.Obama also criticised Trump over the cost of living, saying the president had failed to deliver on a key campaign promise to make life more affordable. Instead, he pointed to Trump's focus on renovating the White House, including plans for a new ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn."I do not know if you have noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," Obama quipped. "He should be on HGTV."He went on, "There is gold everywhere. He is got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."Obama campaigns across key battleground statesObama, 65, remains a prominent campaigner for the Democratic Party and was due to travel to Michigan later on Saturday to support Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official running against Republican former Representative Mike Rogers.El-Sayed won a divisive Democratic primary by less than one percentage point. Obama's appearance in Detroit, a city with a predominantly Black population, could help El-Sayed strengthen his support among Black voters. During the primary, his rival Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about six percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for El-Sayed in September.El-Sayed has previously criticised Obama's record, arguing in 2012 that the former president had failed to fulfil all his progressive campaign promises. He wrote that Obama "was not the right choice -- he just wasn't the wrong one".However, El-Sayed later described Obama as "foundational" to his decision to enter politics, while acknowledging that he still disagreed with parts of the former president's record.Michigan also has competitive elections for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson is facing Republican Representative John James.In Ohio, Obama appeared with Acton and former Senator Sherrod Brown, who is seeking to unseat Republican Senator Jon Husted. Trump and Vance have visited the state in recent weeks to campaign for Husted and Ramaswamy.Obama is also scheduled to headline a rally in Georgia next week with Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is due to speak in Georgia on Saturday.Obama urges voters to reject Republican leadershipAcknowledging that Trump would remain president for another two years, until his term ends, Obama urged voters to use the midterm elections to challenge Republican leaders."We are not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said."After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence ... you get a chance to say enough is enough."You use AI every day. articles.title: A Scottish couple turned their home into a hedgehog hospital; by 2025, they had treated more than 622 hedgehogs
articles.summary: Sharon and Andy Longhurst have turned their home in Burntisland, Fife, Scotland, into a rescue facility for sick, injured and orphaned hedgehogs.
articles.body: Sharon and Andy Longhurst have turned their home in Burntisland, Fife, Scotland, into a rescue facility for sick, injured and orphaned hedgehogs. Sharon works as a school crossing guard, while Andy is a bus driver, but outside their regular jobs, the couple devote much of their time to caring for the small mammals. Their home has been adapted to accommodate different stages of treatment and rehabilitation, with a garage serving as an intensive-care area, a shed providing rehabilitation space and part of the garden used as a maternity ward. By November 2025, the couple had treated more than 622 hedgehogs, according to The Washington Post. Their work is supported by volunteers who help transport animals and assist with their care.How two encounters inspired a wildlife rescue centreThe couple's rescue journey began after they encountered hedgehogs that needed help. In 2022, they found an unwell hedgehog near Kirkcaldy and contacted the Scottish SPCA, but could not arrange a collection. They drove the animal to a wildlife hospital in Alloa, making a round trip of roughly 50 miles.About two weeks later, they came across another hedgehog in need of assistance. The experiences made them realise how difficult it could be for local residents to get help for animals without travelling long distances.They established Burntisland Hedgehog Haven in March 2023, creating a local facility where sick, injured and orphaned hedgehogs could receive care. The operation grew as word spread that the couple were taking in animals needing help.Their home has become a specialised care facilityThe Longhursts gradually adapted their property to meet the needs of the hedgehogs. The garage became an intensive-care area equipped with heated incubators and microscopes, while a shed was converted into a rehabilitation space. The garden was also adapted to accommodate a maternity area for hedgehogs raising young.The facility allows the couple to care for animals at different stages of recovery. The number admitted varies according to the season, the animals' needs and the centre's capacity. The couple have reported being licensed to care for up to 40 hedgehogs at a time.Their home-based operation provides a local option for people who find hedgehogs that are sick, injured or too young to survive without assistance.Feeding orphaned hoglets and treating injured animalsYoung hedgehogs, known as hoglets, often need intensive care when they lose their mothers or become separated from them. The smallest animals require warmth, regular feeding and close monitoring, as their condition can deteriorate quickly.Sharon oversees much of the daily care, including feeding, monitoring the animals' weight and condition, and keeping track of their progress. Some hedgehogs need medication and extended recovery periods, while others require veterinary treatment.The workload can be demanding, particularly during busy periods when several young animals arrive at once. The couple balance these responsibilities with their regular employment, relying on careful routines and help from volunteers to keep the operation running.Volunteers help transport and care for hedgehogsBurntisland Hedgehog Haven depends on community support as well as the couple's own work. Volunteers help with cleaning enclosures, preparing food, weighing animals, administering prescribed medication and maintaining care records.The rescue also has a network of drivers who transport hedgehogs from where they are found to the centre. The informal network is known as the 'hogbulance', a playful combination of 'hog' and 'ambulance'.The transport network helps people who find injured animals but cannot bring them to the centre themselves. It also extends the rescue's reach beyond Burntisland into surrounding parts of Fife.More than 622 hedgehogs treated by November 2025By November 2025, the couple had treated more than 622 hedgehogs, according to The Washington Post. The centre reported that around 65% of the animals it treated survived and were released back into the wild.The outcomes depend on each animal's condition when it arrives. Some recover with food, warmth and time, while others need more extensive medical attention. Animals that are released are returned to suitable locations once they are healthy enough to survive independently.Not every hedgehog can be returned to the wild. The work involves assessing whether an animal has recovered sufficiently to forage, move around and avoid danger without human assistance.Why hedgehogs need conservation supportThe European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) was classified as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List in October 2024, reflecting concerns about population declines across parts of its range.Hedgehogs face several pressures, including habitat loss and fragmentation, road traffic, changes in agricultural practices and declining access to invertebrate prey. Gardens can provide valuable shelter and feeding areas, but hazards such as garden machinery, chemicals and barriers between green spaces can put the animals at risk.Wildlife rehabilitation centres cannot resolve these broader problems alone, but they can help individual animals recover from injuries and illness. The Longhursts also encourage people to make gardens safer for wildlife and to seek specialist help when they find a hedgehog that appears sick or injured.Keeping the rescue operation runningCaring for hundreds of hedgehogs requires food, bedding, heating, medical supplies and equipment. The centre relies on donations and community support to meet these costs, alongside the time contributed by the couple and volunteers.In June 2026, the centre announced a temporary pause on new admissions after a surge in poorly and critically ill hedgehogs pushed it to its permitted capacity. The team continued to offer advice while focusing on animals already in its care.The pause highlighted the limits of a small, home-based rescue operation, even one supported by a committed local network. Each new admission requires space, time and appropriate care, particularly when an animal needs intensive treatment.Taking the hedgehog message beyond FifeThe Longhursts' work attracted wider attention after The Washington Post profiled their home-based rescue in November 2025. Their unusual arrangement, with parts of their home adapted for intensive care and rehabilitation, helped draw attention to the effort required to look after injured wildlife.The couple have also used public appearances and educational outreach to explain the challenges hedgehogs face and how members of the public can help. Their work combines direct care for individual animals with advice intended to make local environments safer for the species.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
articles.summary: Ukraine needs another satellite internet service, but a decent alternative to Elon Musk's network doesn't exist - yet.
articles.body:
Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.

Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.

There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.

France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared to Starlink's 10,000-plus.

The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029.

For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death.

"God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."

For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.

Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?

Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?

Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.

Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks.

"You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations.

Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored , highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate.

"Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.

Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Elon Musk.

While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS.

"This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."

Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to, agree.

Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield," a soldier said.

The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.

Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones," said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.

They are also about five times more expensive, she added.

Rhetoric from the White House - like Donald Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC.

She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.

Comments from Elon Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.

Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently," a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.

Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.

But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.

That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.

Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing, because as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.

Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".

No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.

But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."

Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris² is up and running in 2029.

The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared ) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.

Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.

It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen.

"Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites."

Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".

A highly-produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity."

So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea.

"Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."

It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare."

But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war."

Iris² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences.

And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases.

Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need " a lot of money".

Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years.

"Even if you gave me €8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained.

Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare.

"Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now."

While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels.

"In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said.

articles.title: Donegal: Brown bears adjusting to new life in Irish countryside
articles.summary: For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year journey from Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.
articles.body:
After years in cramped cages, two brown bears are adjusting to their new life following a remarkable rescue mission that spanned multiple countries, was disrupted by two major conflicts and involved more than 100 people.

For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year rescue journey from the Republic of Dagestan in Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.

One bear had spent their life forced to perform in a circus, while the other was confined to a cage so small they could not stand upright.

Today, the bears are now adjusting to a totally different world among the trees and grass at Wild Ireland, a sanctuary for rescued animals in County Donegal.

Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin first learned about Bu and Tyapa in 2021 and committed to bringing them to safety in Donegal.

The sanctuary, located in Burnfoot, opened in October 2019 and provides a safe space for animals, including brown bears, monkeys, wolves, and lynx.

McLaughlin said the two bears were in extremely poor health when they were first rescued.

Former circus bear Bu had spent years confined to a small indoor cage after being forced to perform.

McLaughlin said Tyapa had lived in a cage measuring just 2.5m by 2.5m by 2m, which was too low for him to stand upright and had no roof, which left him exposed to the harsh winters and blistering summer heat.

The bear had no water dish and relied on a hose for drinking water. McLaughlin said he was being raised to be killed for an eventual taxidermy display.

When the bears were rescued, both were severely malnourished and showed signs of psychological trauma.

Blood tests also revealed serious kidney problems associated with prolonged dehydration.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made the original transport route through Ukraine impossible, said McLaughlin.

An alternative route through the Middle East was then explored, but plans were disrupted again in February 2026 when the escalating conflict involving Iran led to airspace closures and flight disruptions across the region.

More than 100 people were involved in the rescue operation, including volunteers, lawyers, veterinarians, animal transport specialists, cargo teams and officials in Russia, the United Arab Emirates and Ireland.

In late October 2025, Dima and Yana Kim, who work at Tiger House, a sanctuary near St Petersburg that cares for former circus tigers, embarked on a 36-hour drive to Dagestan to rescue the bears.

Bu and Tyapa had to be cut out of their rusting steel cages, sedated and placed in secure transport crates for the journey back to Tiger House, where they received veterinary treatment and underwent quarantine.

After months of preparation and repeated delays, the bears eventually travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in Ireland in August.

Since arriving at Wild Ireland, McLaughlin said both bears have gained weight, their coats have improved, and follow-up blood tests have shown that their kidney function has returned to normal.

He said their habitat provides woodland, water and room to explore, as well as sheltered areas where they can retreat or move out of public view if they would like some privacy.

"These bears have suffered trauma and the first step of that recovery process is get them back out into the forest, get their paws into the soil and on the grass and get them exploring.

"We hope they can now have a full and happy life."

Working with bears isn't your normal 9-5

Working with bears is certainly not your everyday job, but for Wild Ireland team member Chloe McElhatton, it's one she absolutely relishes.

Chloe has been working at Wild Ireland for just over a year. She studied zoology at Queen's University Belfast, completing a four-year degree before joining the team.

"This is obviously a very unique job, and it's quite different from what most people would do," she said.

"We've done a lot of work hiding food around the bear habitats, encouraging them to search and forage for it themselves and this promotes their natural behaviours and helps them become more comfortable in that new open space," she said.

"Over time, we've seen their confidence build, and you can see great changes, both physically and mentally, in both of them."

Liam, who is from France, said the bears were one of his favourite animals to see when visiting the park.

"Very big and very impressive," is how he summed up Bu and Tyapa.

"I saw chickens, some wolves and some monkeys and then the bears which were definitely my favourite."

Chris Roberts is from Manorcunningham, about 20 minutes from Wild Ireland, and has been visiting the site ever since it first opened in 2019.

"I've lost count of how many times we've been here, but we really wanted to come down today to see if we could catch a glimpse of Bu and Tyapa.

"It was fantastic to see them in the flesh.

"We absolutely loved it and are delighted to see them doing so well, especially considering their backstory and the awful conditions they were once kept in."

articles.title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
articles.summary: Scotland editor James Cook finds out what life is like on board a ship in an untapped oil field awaiting its fate.
articles.body:
When we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.

We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.

But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic – the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.

This summer, along with a camera crew, I travelled to Jackdaw, 150 miles east of Aberdeen.

Now we were the first journalists to visit Rosebank.

We came here - days before Storm Boelo arrived with strong winds and heavy rain - to scrutinise a controversial project which is at the heart of a national debate about climate change, energy policy and the economy.

But we also hoped for a rare glimpse into life offshore.

"It's good fun, it's interesting, every day can change," said Nicola Boyd, who runs the helideck, and greeted us as we struggled out of our lifejackets and survival suits.

Boyd has worked offshore for nearly a decade, including a year on Rosebank - where she spends two weeks at a time followed by three weeks' leave.

It's also a job that calls for steady legs and a strong stomach.

Unlike the fixed Jackdaw platform, this installation – 80 miles north west of Shetland – is a large ship, a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO) named the Petrojarl Rosebank.

It's been chartered by the field's owners from Aberdeen-based Altera and, during my 48 hours on board, it was constantly but gently rolling on the North Atlantic swell.

With the understatement typical of an Orkney islander, lead mechanical technician Ewan Leonard told me the winter weather could be "a bit of a challenge."

"Last week we had a 30m heave coming through," he said, referring to the swell, "so we'll probably suffer more of that as the winter goes on."

Altera CEO Chris Brett told me that in the industry the environment west of Shetland is considered "as harsh as you get anywhere in the world."

Whatever your view on that industry, the sheer scale of what humans have achieved in such conditions is impressive.

The deep reserves of skill, ingenuity and engineering prowess among the 122 people on board are obvious.

The jobs are well-paid and, according to Ewan Leonard, the facilities are excellent.

"We have single-man cabins, there's good gym facilities, there's a lot of rec rooms here."

Douglas Hogge, a production supervisor in charge of a team responsible for the safe extraction of oil and gas, agrees.

"There's the gym, the sauna," he said, adding "you can obviously go and get some fresh air. There's plenty of fresh air out there."

"As you've seen yourself, the food is fantastic on board, so no complaints." added Leonard.

Everyone we spoke to agreed with that, praising the talented chefs who sent out all sorts of delicious dishes, from braised ox cheek to mackerel to pork loin, day and night.

As dusk gathers and the nightshift get ready for work with a strange breakfast of fillet steak and chocolate brownie pudding, the vessel begins to glow in the gloom.

It is a strange sight, the decks criss-crossed by a bewilderingly complex array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork.

The ship doesn't move far, rotating around a fixed central point called the turret to face into the weather, making life a little easier for those on board.

If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through the turret from wells in the field below, which contains an estimated 300m to 500m barrels, enough for perhaps 25 years.

"For myself and a lot of the guys, that would see us out to retirement," said Douglas Hogge.

"We need to see this approved," he added.

Environmental campaigners strongly disagree. They've been trying to stop Rosebank for years, with some success.

"The future of the energy sector in the UK is renewable energy," said Tessa Khan, executive director of the campaigning group Uplift.

Consent for production at Rosebank was first granted under the Conservative government in 2023.

But in 2025, after a challenge by Greenpeace and Uplift, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled the approvals of the UK's largest known untapped oil field and Jackdaw were unlawful because they had failed to take into account the climate impact of actually burning the fossil fuels in cars, homes and factories.

The judge, Lord Ericht, said the fields' developers could carry on with work short of producing oil and gas while they provided more detailed environmental assessments for the government and regulators to consider.

"We think Rosebank would be a disastrous decision and a terrible deal for ordinary people across this country," said Khan, urging prime minister Andy Burnham to prioritise renewables in his quest to re-industrialise the nation.

"If the government's interested in building investor confidence, giving the green light to a major new oil field is going to do the opposite," she argued.

Whatever happens with Rosebank and Jackdaw, the long-term trend for the industry is clear and it is one of decline.

It's a quarter of a century since oil production peaked and in recent years jobs in oil and gas have been disappearing much faster than they're being created in renewable energy such as wind and solar power.

The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle, which looks like the super-sized pump of an enormous floating filling station.

From there it would be sold on the international market and, most likely, taken to continental Europe for refining.

Opponents say that proves the project is of little benefit to the UK and should be rejected.

Supporters argue that's not the case because UK and European energy markets are co-dependent, adding that Rosebank will generate millions in tax for the Treasury.

Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura – which owns 80% of Rosebank and is a joint venture between Shell and the Norwegian state energy firm, Equinor – is optimistic.

He points out that Rosebank contains not just oil but gas which would be piped to Shetland and on to the St Fergus terminal in Aberdeenshire, with the potential to heat 500,000 British homes at peak production.

Approval of this project, argues McCulloch, could pave the way for four more Jackdaw-sized gas developments in the waters west of Shetland – Tornado, Tornado East, Tobermory and Suilven.

"We would like to proceed with them," he said.

A surge in fossil fuel production if Rosebank is approved is exactly what campaigners fear.

It would, argues Tessa Khan, exacerbate the deadly and damaging impact of climate change for British teachers, nurses, firefighters and families worried about their children while making "huge profits for companies that are already incredibly profitable".

When it comes to the impending UK government decision – which sources have told BBC News should come before Christmas – there is a strange mood at Rosebank.

The decision in favour of Jackdaw has clearly encouraged many on board but it has also highlighted the jeopardy they are facing.

For now, most workers we spoke to said they were just focusing on the job, with its strange rhythms and unusual restrictions – no ability to pop to the shops, no alcohol, a lot of special occasions missed.

And for some on board, very particular cravings.

For steward Liam Davidson, it is a desire to see his French bulldog, Bailey, at the end of his fortnight on board.

"My wee dog's at the heliport when I arrive," he said, "I do miss her."

For Nicola Boyd, it's her double bed and a pizza delivery.

"I love seeing the family, but for me, it's the pizza," she told me.

But this time there might be a delay in delivering Boyd herself.

She is coming to the end of her fortnight but, as she helped us into our survival suits, the Met Office issued an amber weather warning for much of Scotland.

For Rosebank, it seems, there are stormy seas ahead, one way or the another.

articles.title: Brazil election: Voters to choose between Lula and Bolsonaro's son
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil's imprisoned former president, is presenting a strong challenge to Lula, 80, who is seeking a fourth term in office.
articles.body:
Brazilians go to the polls on Sunday to elect their new president in a closely fought run-off election.

The choice is between the 80-year-old incumbent, left-winger Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term in office, and right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45.

Bolsonaro is the son of former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the last election in 2022.

This is Bolsonaro's election to lose after he came top in the first round of voting on 4 October, which US President Donald Trump called a "very big" victory.

Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.

Bolsonaro's supporters were jubilant at his final campaign rallies, confident that he would bring change to Brazil through his promised tough crackdown on organised crime, as well as tax and public spending cuts.

He campaigned on the eve of polls in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, which has been a must-win state for any presidential hopeful since the 1980s.

"The time is almost here," Bolsonaro told supporters in a social media video.

"There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years."

He has also pledged to release his father, who is currently serving his sentence under house arrest due to ill health.

In Barra de Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, where Jair Bolsonaro has a home, Bolsonaro supporters rallied in support of him dressed in the national colours.

"Brazil needs change, and Flávio is the person that represents that today, after so many years of the Left destroying the economy and the country," one told BBC News.

Another said that what she most liked about Flávio Bolsonaro was his promise to "end violence in Brazil, end terrorism, narco-trafficking, and to reduce interest rates".

Since Bolsonaro's first-round victory, supporters of Lula have arranged huge rallies in support of him to try to boost turnout after 33 million people did not cast a vote earlier this month.

On Saturday, Lula told a huge crowd on Rio de Janeiro's Copacabana beach that this election was a matter of "sovereignty" and people would choose between the one who kissed the Brazilian flag or the American flag.

Lula's administration has accused the US of interfering in Brazil's election , an allegation Washington has called "baseless".

"We're going to win the election for one simple reason: it's true that the people want change [but] they want to move forward," he said. "They don't want to go backward."

A supporter called Roberta told BBC News: "This movement is to show we have strength. We've woken up, we're coming to the street to make a difference and turn the vote around."

A man wearing Brazil's national yellow and green football shirt said Bolsonaro supporters had "appropriated" the jersey but Lula supporters were taking it back.

How Brazil's changing working class is reshaping the presidential race

What to know about Brazil's run-off as Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro face off

Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote

Personal attacks fire up debate before Brazil's run-off vote

Lula and his Workers' Party have cast this election as a "battle for democracy", arguing that Jair Bolsonaro's conviction for coup-plotting is evidence that "Bolsonarismo" constitutes a threat to Brazil's democratic institutions.

During Lula's latest term in office, relations with Trump have been rocky.

Lula has insisted that Brazil "does not fit into anyone's backyard", an apparent reference to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with.

Bolsonaro, on the other hand, argues that working with Washington to combat powerful criminal gangs - which wield immense power in parts of Brazil - will restore the state's sovereignty to gang-controlled areas.

He has also been labelling the Workers' Party as corrupt, reminding voters of the massive financial scandals which plagued the party for years and which have turned many voters against it.

Lula plans to be in São Paulo to watch the results on Sunday evening while Bolsonaro is set to be in the capital Brasília - which is also where his father is under house arrest.

articles.summary: 2º turno terá chuva forte em São Paulo, Paraná e Mato Grosso do Sul. Há risco de temporais e ventos de até 90 km/h. Norte e Nordeste terão predomínio de calor.
articles.body:
O segundo turno das eleições de 2026, neste domingo (25), deve ser de chuva forte em parte do Sul, do Sudeste e do Centro-Oeste durante o período de votação, das 8h às 17h , pelo horário de Brasília.

Segundo a Climatempo, São Paulo deve concentrar as chuvas mais intensas durante a manhã. Há previsão de pancadas fortes desde as primeiras horas do dia .

Também pode chover forte no Paraná, principalmente nas regiões central, norte e leste, e em Mato Grosso do Sul, onde há possibilidade de temporais ao longo de todo o domingo .

Depois do meio-dia, as pancadas devem atingir outras áreas do Sudeste, principalmente Minas Gerais e Espírito Santo. No Norte e no Nordeste, o sol e o calor devem predominar , com temperaturas que podem chegar aos 40°C.

No Centro-Sul, a previsão está associada à formação de um ciclone extratropical e ao avanço de uma frente fria , que já provocou temporais neste sábado (24) e que neste domingo deve alcançar uma área maior do Sudeste.

🌀 ENTENDA: Os ciclones extratropicais são sistemas de baixa pressão atmosférica – regiões causadoras de tempo adverso em grande escala – que surgem normalmente em latitudes médias. Eles são formados pelo contraste de temperaturas de diferentes massas de ar (quente e fria).

Pela manhã, São Paulo, Paraná e Mato Grosso do Sul devem concentrar as áreas com maior possibilidade de chuva forte.

No estado paulista, a chuva pode atingir a capital, o litoral e diferentes regiões do interior desde a madrugada.

Segundo César Soares, meteorologista da Climatempo, a previsão é de chuva intensa nessas áreas.

"Temos previsão para bastante chuva, com raios e ventos fortes", afirma César.

No Paraná, os maiores volumes são esperados no centro, norte e leste do estado, incluindo a Região Metropolitana de Curitiba.

Em Santa Catarina, a chuva também pode ser forte durante a madrugada e a manhã , principalmente no litoral e no Vale do Itajaí.

No Rio de Janeiro, a previsão indica chuva desde cedo , especialmente na Região Metropolitana, na Costa Verde e na Região Serrana. Também pode chover em pontos do sul de Minas Gerais.

Já no Rio Grande do Sul, a chuva tende a ser mais fraca e passageira , com muitas nuvens durante o domingo.

🌧️ Entre as capitais, a Climatempo prevê chuva na manhã deste domingo (25) em:

São Paulo (SP), Rio de Janeiro (RJ), Curitiba (PR) e Campo Grande (MS), onde há possibilidade de chuva moderada a forte.

Porto Alegre (RS), onde a chuva deve ser mais fraca e pode ocorrer em diferentes momentos do dia.

Florianópolis (SC), que pode registrar pancadas mais intensas em alguns períodos da manhã.

À tarde, a chuva deve continuar em parte do Centro-Sul e ganhar força em outras áreas do Sudeste.

Em Minas Gerais, as pancadas podem atingir principalmente o sul do estado, a Zona da Mata e a região central.

No Espírito Santo, a chuva pode ganhar força e provocar temporais no centro-sul capixaba.

articles.title: In 2018, fertiliser and ant killer in a Florida garage spontaneously combusted; appeals court revived the homeowner's compensation claim
articles.summary: In September 2018, fertiliser and red ant killer stored in a Florida garage spontaneously combusted, causing damage to a home and its contents.
articles.body: In September 2018, fertiliser and red ant killer stored in a Florida garage spontaneously combusted, causing damage to a home and its contents. What followed was a lengthy insurance dispute that continued even after the homeowner’s insurer became insolvent. Nearly 8 years later, a Florida appeals court overturned decisions that prevented the homeowner from pursuing compensation for his damaged belongings and presenting evidence of the full extent of his losses. The ruling allows the dispute to return to a lower court, where the claim can be considered again.How did the Florida garage fire lead to a compensation disputeAccording to the Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal’s ruling in Sam Florio v. Florida Insurance Guaranty Association, the fire occurred at Sam Florio’s home in New Smyrna Beach, Florida, in September 2018. The spontaneous combustion of fertiliser and red ant killer in his garage damaged both the property and its contents.Florio had a home insurance policy with Southern Fidelity Insurance Company. In addition to covering damage to the building and additional living expenses, the policy included up to $159,000 in cover for personal belongings. He had also paid an additional premium to insure those belongings at their replacement cost, rather than having depreciation deducted from their value.After the fire, the insurer hired Servpro to carry out restoration work and prepare an inventory of the damaged contents. However, Florio became dissatisfied with the company’s business practices and dismissed it before the work was completed.The insurer paid a combined $54,800.66 to Florio and Servpro, but the parties could not agree on the total value of the losses. As reported by Insurance Business, the disagreement eventually became a legal battle over the evidence needed to support his claim.What happened after the original insurer became insolventFlorio filed a breach of contract lawsuit against Southern Fidelity in February 2019. The insurer accepted that the losses were covered under the policy but disputed their extent and value.The legal proceedings were subsequently paused after Southern Fidelity became insolvent and entered liquidation. The Florida Insurance Guaranty Association, commonly known as FIGA, was then substituted as the defendant.FIGA is a public, non-profit organisation established to help pay eligible insurance claims when covered insurers become insolvent. However, its payments are subject to a statutory limit.According to the court judgment, the case eventually reached a jury trial in January 2025. By then, Florio’s lawyer had withdrawn, leaving him to present his case without legal representation.He described the damage caused by the fire, showed photographs of the affected property and produced receipts for items he had replaced. He also maintained records of the work carried out on the house and explained the belongings that had been discarded.These included appliances, a kayak, two all-terrain vehicles, food, spices and clothing. He also presented photographs showing items kept in his freezers, including animals stored for food and taxidermy.The missing inventory became a major issueThe main difficulty was that Florio had not supplied a complete inventory identifying every damaged item and its replacement value. FIGA argued that his evidence was insufficient to establish ownership and prove the amount of his personal property losses.Florio told the court that he had inventoried approximately 90% of the contents. He said he had established replacement values for many items using receipts, personal knowledge and his own research.The court record also explains that Servpro had moved the garage contents into 6 portable storage containers. Months later, experts hired by both parties examined the items and concluded that they were all rubbish. The contents were subsequently disposed of.As reported on LAWS website in its coverage of the dispute, FIGA maintained that the absence of a complete inventory made the claim too uncertain. The trial court accepted that argument and granted a directed verdict against Florio on his personal property claim, effectively preventing the jury from awarding compensation for those losses.A directed verdict is a decision made by a judge to resolve a claim without allowing the jury to decide it because the evidence is considered legally insufficient.What did the appeals court decide about the evidenceThe Fifth District Court of Appeal disagreed with the lower court’s decision. In its ruling dated 2 October 2026, it concluded that Florio had presented enough evidence for his personal property claim to proceed.According to the judgment, the fact that he lacked a complete professional inventory did not automatically make his evidence inadequate. Florio had testified about his belongings, explained what had been damaged and presented photographs and receipts that could help establish the losses.Insurance Business reported that FIGA had agreed to admit the homeowner’s proposed exhibits before later arguing that the evidence was insufficient. The appeals court found that the association could not simply disregard the consequences of that agreement.The court also considered the significance of the replacement-cost provision in Florio’s insurance policy. Because he had paid extra for replacement-cost coverage, he was not required to establish the depreciated value of every damaged item in the same way as a policyholder insured only for actual cash value.The ruling did not establish that Florio was entitled to every amount he claimed. Instead, it determined that his evidence should have been considered rather than having the entire personal property claim dismissed.Why does the $500,000 compensation limit matterA second issue concerned FIGA’s statutory limit of $500,000. Before the trial began, the association had sought to prevent Florio from presenting evidence of total damages exceeding that amount. The trial court granted the request.Florio argued that the limit on the amount he could ultimately recover should not prevent him from showing the full extent of his losses.The appeals court agreed. As explained in the judgment the statutory ceiling limits recovery rather than the amount of evidence a claimant may present.This distinction matters because the full value of a loss and the amount legally recoverable from FIGA are not necessarily the same. Evidence of damages exceeding the statutory limit can still be relevant even if the final payment remains subject to that ceiling.The appeals court reversed the decision dismissing the personal property claim and vacated the order restricting evidence of damages beyond the statutory cap. The case will return to the lower court for further proceedings. Florio will have another opportunity to present evidence supporting his claim for damaged belongings, although the ruling does not guarantee a particular award.You use AI every day. Macaé TEC estreia na Semana de Ciência e Tecnologia no Centro de
Convenções | G1
articles.standfirst: Evento gratuito reunirá atrações tecnológicas, jogos e experiências imersivas de 26 a 28 de novembro.
articles.summary: Evento gratuito reunirá atrações tecnológicas, jogos e experiências imersivas de 26 a 28 de novembro.
articles.body:
Centro de Convenções sediará a primeira edição do Macaé TEC em novembro — Foto: Arquivo Secom

O município de Macaé promoverá em novembro a primeira edição do Macaé TEC, evento realizado pela Secretaria Municipal Executiva de Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação em alusão à Semana Nacional de Ciência e Tecnologia. A programação acontecerá entre os dias 26 e 28 de novembro (de quinta-feira a sábado), no Centro de Convenções Jornalista Roberto Marinho, no Bairro São José do Barreto.

Com entrada e estacionamento gratuitos todos os dias, o evento não exige inscrição prévia, permitindo que os interessados compareçam diretamente ao local. No sábado (28), a programação será incrementada pelas atrações do Experience X e do XGames 2026, que prosseguirão até o domingo (29) com competições esportivas de cross e diversas experiências interativas.

A proposta do Macaé TEC é aproximar a ciência e a inovação do cotidiano da população de forma acessível e dinamicamente integrada. A organização prepara uma série de atrações tecnológicas e atividades imersivas voltadas para crianças, jovens e adultos, com o objetivo de despertar a curiosidade e demonstrar na prática como a evolução científica contribui para o desenvolvimento social.

A criação do Macaé TEC simboliza o compromisso do município com o fortalecimento das políticas públicas do setor e o incentivo ao conhecimento. A iniciativa reforça a posição da cidade como referência em inovação na região, unindo aprendizado e entretenimento para todas as idades.

articles.title: Twitch streamer Frogan seeks $73,000 in donations after Ethan Klein voluntarily dismisses copyright lawsuit
articles.summary: Twitch streamer Morgan Frogan is asking supporters for financial help after a lengthy copyright dispute with YouTuber Ethan Klein left her facing a
articles.body: Twitch streamer Morgan Frogan is asking supporters for financial help after a lengthy copyright dispute with YouTuber Ethan Klein left her facing a $73,000 legal bill. Although Klein’s company has voluntarily dismissed the lawsuit, the financial strain has not disappeared. Frogan says she has already spent more than $100,000 on legal costs and wants to settle the remaining amount so she can move forward. Her fundraising appeal has drawn fresh attention to the personal and financial consequences of online disputes that escalate into legal battles.Frogan seeks $73,000 to cover legal fees after Ethan Klein lawsuitFrogan took to X to explain her financial situation and ask followers to contribute to her legal expenses. She said the litigation had placed her under serious financial pressure, even though the company behind Klein’s lawsuit has since withdrawn the case.“I still owe $73K after it costing well over $100K.”She followed the post with a direct appeal to supporters.“Please donate to help cover my legal fees, so that I do not have to think about Ethan ever again.”Frogan also shared a link to her GoFundMe campaign, which seeks to raise $200,000. At the time of the report, the fundraiser had collected $45,491.In the campaign description, Frogan alleged that the dispute followed a prolonged period of harassment and said the lawsuit concerned her reaction to Klein’s video about Hasan Piker and herself, titled “Content Nuke - Hasan Piker.”The fundraiser is intended to cover legal bills linked to the complaint, possible counterclaims and other expenses, including lost wages and damages arising from the litigation.Ethan Klein’s copyright lawsuit dismissal leaves questions over Frogan’s caseThe legal dispute began in June 2025, when Ethan Klein accused Frogan and fellow online personalities Denims and Kacey “Kaceytron” of copyright infringement over reaction content related to his video.On September 8, 2026, Ted Entertainment, Inc., Klein’s company, voluntarily dismissed the proceedings without prejudice. This means the company may be able to bring the case again, so the dismissal does not necessarily end the dispute permanently.Frogan addressed the development in a September 9 post on X, expressing hope that the decision would bring the prolonged legal fight to a close.“On September 8, 2026, I woke up to the news that Ethan Klein had voluntarily dismissed his lawsuit against me after more than a year,” Frogan wrote.She also acknowledged that the dismissal could leave the door open for the lawsuit to be filed again.“Of course, I want to be hopeful that it means the end of the lawsuit, which has taken an enormous toll on me,” she added.Frogan has maintained that her use of Klein’s video qualified as fair use and thanked those who supported her throughout the proceedings. For now, the fundraiser highlights the costs she says remain even after the legal action was withdrawn.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A 27-year-old Minnesota man saw a school bus carrying 19 children rolling with its doors open, jumped aboard despite never driving one and stopped it after the driver suffered a medical emergency
articles.summary: A routine afternoon in St. Paul took a frightening turn when a school bus began moving through the streets with its driver incapacitated.
articles.body: A routine afternoon in St. Paul took a frightening turn when a school bus began moving through the streets with its driver incapacitated. With 19 middle school students on board and no one apparently in control of the vehicle, a nearby business owner found himself facing a split-second decision, run toward the bus or watch it continue down the road.According to ABC News, Ebro Ahmed, 27, was taking a break outside his family-owned business, Ya Bricks Snacks & Tobacco, in the Dayton's Bluff neighbourhood when he noticed the Battle Creek Middle School bus travelling with its doors open. What he saw inside prompted him to act immediately.A bus without a driver in controlAccording to ABC News and the New York Post, Ahmed noticed that something was wrong with the driver as the bus moved slowly through the area. The vehicle was reportedly travelling at around 10 mph, giving Ahmed enough time to catch up.He ran toward the moving bus and climbed aboard. Ahmed had never driven a school bus before, but with the children still inside and the vehicle continuing forward, he attempted to bring it under control. His first attempt did not go entirely as planned. He reversed the bus instead of parking. After switching to neutral and setting the parking brake, the bus stopped.Protecting studentsAhmed faced the children and driver when the bus stopped. He helped the disabled driver and told students to call 911. The 19 students were not physically injured, although the sudden incident left some of them frightened. Reports described children preparing to call 911 and reacting anxiously as the situation unfolded.Ahmed's actions prevented the bus from continuing uncontrolled through the neighbourhood, turning what could have become a far more serious incident into an emergency response rather than a potential crash. Fox34 reported that the incident occurred Monday and involved a contracted route serving Battle Creek Middle School.A situation he never expectedAhmed later acknowledged that he had no formal training in operating a school bus. His response instead came from trying to remain calm and recalling things he had seen before. Among the unexpected influences he credited was the medical drama Grey's Anatomy, along with videos encountered online. Rather than panic, he tried to concentrate on the immediate problem and work through the controls.The St. Paul Public Schools district said the driver's medical emergency likely caused delays for students returning home. Some children were also upset by what had happened, prompting the district's mental health team to check in with students following the incident.Driver released from hospitalThe bus driver was taken to a hospital following the medical emergency and was later released to recover at home, according to school officials, states the ABC News report.Ahmed said the episode was particularly personal because he could easily imagine the children being members of his own family. His decision to intervene, therefore, was less about recognition and more about protecting a group of children who suddenly found themselves in an unpredictable and potentially dangerous situation.The incident has since drawn widespread attention online, with Ahmed being praised for his quick response. What began as an ordinary break outside a neighbourhood business ended with an untrained bystander taking control of a moving school bus and helping ensure that all 19 students made it through a frightening journey safely.Images Courtesy: ABC NewsYou use AI every day. articles.title: 'Lie and fabrication': Iran denies Hormuz deal offer to US through Pakistan
articles.summary: Iran has denied reports that it offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in return for the US lifting its naval blockade, with the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim
articles.body: Iran has denied reports that it offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in return for the US lifting its naval blockade, with the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency saying Tehran has made no fresh proposal to Pakistani mediators.Citing sources, Tasnim said reports by a Saudi Arabian outlet claiming that Iran had conveyed such an offer to Washington through Pakistan were “a lie and fabrication", Press TV reported.The reports had suggested that Tehran was willing to reopen the strategic waterway if the US ended its naval blockade.On October 18, Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi had said Tehran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days remained on the table. He made the remarks while speaking to Iranian media in Baghdad.“Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to ​the ​US. They shared comments which we ⁠are reviewing… If there is any ‌honesty on the US part, which there isn’t, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious,” he said.The denial comes as US President Donald Trump has maintained that a deal with Iran remains possible, while keeping the option of further military action open. He has insisted that any agreement must permanently prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.Trump also threatened fresh military action against Iran if it fails to reach a diplomatic agreement with Washington, suggesting that the US could launch "another little Epic Fury".Speaking at a campaign rally in Florida, Trump adopted a hardline stance towards Tehran, referring to previous US military action and warning that further strikes remained an option if negotiations failed."We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," Trump told the cheering crowd.Questioning Iran's willingness to negotiate, he added, "If they're smart, they'll just say, 'Let's get down to business. But, you know, I doubt they'll do that because perhaps they're not smart."Iran claims full control over Strait of HormuzAmid the escalating rhetoric, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Saturday claimed that Iran retained full control over the Strait of Hormuz, adding that vessels operating in the region were being provided security in accordance with Iranian regulations.The IRGC Navy also alleged that two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels of crude oil combined had struck naval mines while attempting to navigate a southern route through the waterway that Tehran described as unauthorised.Iran has separately warned that it would not allow US military vessels to enter the Persian Gulf, pushing back against Washington's claims that Iranian military capabilities had been significantly weakened.According to Iranian state broadcaster Press TV, Major General Ali Abdollahi, chief of the general staff of Iran's armed forces, said Iranian forces had rendered the US Navy ineffective in the region."The US president must only dream of their military and army entering the Persian Gulf again. They will take this wish to their graves," Abdollahi said."We will under no circumstances and at no time allow US military vessels to enter the Persian Gulf," he added.Abdollahi also challenged Trump's repeated assertions that Iran's nuclear facilities had been destroyed, questioning why Washington continued to express concerns over Tehran's nuclear programme if the facilities had already been eliminated.You use AI every day. articles.title: In first-ever climate crisis amends, Nepal to get $21.6 million
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Marking its first response to a climate change-induced loss and damage event, a UN body has decided to provide $21.6 million to Nepal that
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Marking its first response to a climate change-induced loss and damage event, a UN body has decided to provide $21.6 million to Nepal that faced catastrophic flash floods in Aug, triggered by a massive rock-ice avalanche and a partial glacier collapse.The decision taken this week by the UN body, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), in its emergency meeting assumes significance as it is not only a kind of admission that climate change causes such extreme events, but also an endorsement of the principle that historical polluters (developed nations) must contribute to the fund to assist vulnerable developing countries.The purpose of this fund, created under the UN climate change framework, is to assist developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change. The fund was established at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, in 2022 and operationalised at COP28 in Dubai, UAE, in 2023.“This is a historic first step, but it cannot be a one-off. No country should have to endure a catastrophe and wait seven weeks just to unlock the Fund’s first-ever emergency meeting. We must set up a permanent rapid-response system that moves support in days, not months,” said Harjeet Singh, a climate change expert and the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign.You use AI every day. articles.title: Violent protests in Arunachal against Siang dam; MLAs’ homes looted, NHPC set ablaze
articles.summary: GUWAHATI/ITANAGAR: Protests against Arunachal Pradesh's proposed 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) turned violent at Pasighat, East Siang
articles.body: GUWAHATI/ITANAGAR: Protests against Arunachal Pradesh's proposed 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) turned violent at Pasighat, East Siang district, on Friday night, with "Gen Z" protesters allegedly torching the NHPC office and a police station, and vandalising and looting the residences of two MLAs and the state BJP president, police said.The violence continued in waves for nearly nine hours early Saturday, leaving "over 40 police personnel injured in stone-pelting", police said. A protester was hit in the leg by a tear gas shell and admitted to hospital. The East Siang district administration imposed restrictions on public gatherings and processions in Pasighat, Mebo and Ruksin, citing apprehensions of vandalism, arson and a potential breach of law and order following protests and bandh-related activities.In an executive order issued Saturday, deputy commissioner Jayanti Pertin said the restrictions would come into effect from 5pm on Oct 24 and remain in force until withdrawn or modified.The violence began after a 12-hour bandh called by Adi Baane Kebang United, along with other organisations, against the proposed project ended peacefully at 5pm. The bandh, however, was not observed in Pasighat area.CM expresses concern, offers to meet groups for talksOne of our deputy SPs suffered a head injury and has been evacuated to Dibrugarh, where he is being treated. Central police force personnel were also badly hurt, Pasighat IGP (central range) Hibu Tamang said.The mob also pelted stones at a hospital where injured central force personnel had been taken. At least nine police vehicles were damaged. The groups dispersed around 4am.“A youth group calling itself ‘Gen Z’ suddenly emerged and sat on a dharna on the Mebo side. Around 2pm, this group entered Pasighat jurisdiction. They blocked the Pasighat-Boleng highway and did not let traffic pass. They had no clear demand. They said they would sit on a dharna indefinitely, and there was also slogan-shouting,” Tamang said.He said police and civil authorities persuaded the group to leave the highway for two hours without any result. “As darkness fell, the group became very violent and unruly. A violent mob of 200-300 began pelting stones at police and the magistrate. Some of them were carrying liquor and beer bottles in their hands and were intoxicated. Police handled it gently and did nothing other than using tear gas,” the IGP said.Police said that they documented the incident on video and photographs.Arunachal Pradesh chief minister Pema Khandu expressed concern and offered to meet the groups for talks.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Guwahati | Silver Rate in Guwahati | Bank Holidays in Guwahati | Public Holidays in Guwahati | Guwahati AQI | Weather in Guwahati | Petrol Price in Guwahati | Diesel Price in Guwahati | CNG Price in Guwahati | LPG Price in GuwahatiStay updated with the latest Guwahati news.
